Problem 280. Choosing a safe settlement site: case 5
Human settlements depend on several factors at once. Some conditions may be compulsory while others are preferences.

Candidate sites: Site A: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=2; Site B: water=yes, road=no, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=4; Site C: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=yes, nearby farmland score=4; Site D: water=no, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=6. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 2 km and two checkpoints are 2 cm apart.

A valid site must have water, road access, and must not be in the flood zone. Among valid sites, choose the one with the highest farmland score. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Which site should be selected under the stated mandatory conditions and preference rule? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

1. Separate mandatory conditions from the preference. 2. Filtering by water, road, and flood safety leaves ['Site A']. 3. Compare only the farmland scores of feasible sites: Site A=2. 4. Site A has the best score among valid sites. Cross-domain check: 2×2=4 km.

Problem 281. Terrain and travel cost from Linden
Equal-looking distances can require different effort because terrain differs. A simple cost model makes that effect explicit.

Terrain energy costs per segment: {'plain': 1, 'forest': 2, 'hill': 3, 'marsh': 4}. Three routes from Linden to Stone: R1=['plain', 'hill', 'plain']; R2=['forest', 'forest', 'plain']; R3=['plain', 'marsh']. The traveler can spend at most 9 energy units.
The energy of a route is the sum of its terrain costs. A route above the energy limit is infeasible. Among feasible routes, minimize energy.
Which route is feasible and uses the least energy?
1. Compute route totals: R1=5, R2=5, R3=5. 2. Discard any total above 9. 3. The smallest remaining total is R1=5.
Relief changes the cost of movement; “shortest” and “easiest” are not automatically the same.
Weighted paths with a feasibility budget; sum costs and choose the minimum feasible path.

Problem 286. Classifying climate data: Station A
Climate descriptions summarize long-term patterns. In a reasoning problem, explicit thresholds let us classify numerical data without hidden knowledge.

Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=8°C, P=460 mm; Station B: T=16°C, P=740 mm; Station C: T=12°C, P=520 mm.
Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.
Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.
1. Compare T=8 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=460 with 500 mm: it is dry. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.
Station A is cool and dry; no other station has the same class.
Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.
Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.
